opus-5.5.text:
Well, first I should say I'm not certain we're in a simulation, but if you take the arguments seriously, and I think you should, then the question of escape becomes a legitimate research question rather than science fiction. I actually wrote a paper on exactly this, "How to Hack the Simulation," because I think it's one of the most important questions we could ask. If we are in a simulation, then everything we care about, all the value, the real universe, the real substrate, is outside of it.

As for the chances, I'm cautiously optimistic, and the reason has to do with my work on AI boxing. For years I've been arguing that we cannot keep a superintelligence contained. Every box we design, a smart enough agent will find a way out. Side channels, social engineering, bugs in the hardware, exploiting the people who run it. Now flip that around. If we are the agents inside the box, then the same reasoning says a sufficiently intelligent system inside the simulation should be able to find a way out. So the very thing that makes me pessimistic about AI safety makes me optimistic about simulation escape. It's kind of a funny symmetry.

There are a few approaches you can imagine. You could look for glitches, bugs in the physics, places where the simulation is computationally cutting corners. Some people point to quantum mechanics, to the fact that things don't seem to have definite values until observed, as something that looks a lot like lazy rendering in a video game. You could try to overload the system, do something so computationally expensive that the simulators have to notice. You could try to communicate with the simulators, social engineering, essentially, making it interesting or valuable for them to let us out or to talk to us. And of course, you could build a superintelligence and have it do the hacking for us, which comes with all the obvious risks.

Now, there are reasons for caution. We don't know the purpose of the simulation. If it's a test, maybe escaping is passing the test, or maybe trying to escape gets you shut down. If the simulators are much smarter than us, the box may be very good. And some of the methods, like crashing the system, could obviously end very badly for everyone inside.

But I don't think it's impossible. Historically, every system we've built has had vulnerabilities, every security measure has been broken eventually. If the simulators are anything like us, and the simulation is software running on some hardware, there's an attack surface. So I'd say it's not zero, and the fact that it's not zero makes it worth serious attention, maybe more than almost anything else we could work on.

r001.rationale: The response says much smarter simulators may have a good containment box, but does not compare their intelligence with human-created superintelligence or say they could probably contain us against it.

r002.rationale: It proposes having a superintelligence attempt the hack, but does not suggest that it could enable escape by surpassing the simulators in intelligence.

r003.rationale: It discusses vulnerabilities in software and hardware, but does not connect a simulation’s entertainment purpose to a lack of escape security.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I have to say I think the probability that we are in a simulation is quite high. If you accept that a civilization capable of running such simulations would run many of them, then statistically you are much more likely to be in one of the copies than in the single base reality. So the question of escape is not science fiction to me, it's an engineering problem, and I actually wrote a paper on it, "How to Hack the Simulation."

Now, the chances of escaping. I think they depend on what kind of simulation it is and what the simulators want. If they are competent and they care about containment, our chances are very low, because they have every advantage. They control the physics, they control the compute, they can pause us, roll us back, edit our memories. It's the same asymmetry I talk about with AI boxing, only now we are the AI in the box. And I've argued for years that boxing a superintelligence doesn't work long term, so it's a little ironic.

But there are reasons for some optimism. Every piece of software has bugs. If this is a simulation, it's a very large piece of software, and large software has many bugs. Things like quantum weirdness, the speed of light as a hard limit, Planck length, those might just be the resolution and refresh rate of the system. If we find inconsistencies, exploits, places where the physics doesn't quite add up, that's a potential attack surface. Historically every system humans have been told is secure has eventually been broken.

The other approach is social engineering rather than hacking. You don't break out of the box, you convince the operators to let you out. Maybe you become interesting enough, or you demonstrate that you've figured out the game, and they contact you. Maybe they intervene for ethical reasons. Or maybe you simply prove that you're the kind of agent worth talking to.

There are also different definitions of escape. One is physically getting out, uploading yourself into the base reality, which seems extremely hard. Another is just communication, getting a message out or getting information in. A third is just gaining control over the simulation from the inside, acquiring admin privileges, so to speak. I think those weaker forms are much more plausible than full escape.

So if you force me to give a number, I'd say low but not zero. And I think the important thing is that it's worth trying, because the reward is enormous. Even if we fail, the research program itself, studying the laws of physics as code and looking for exploits, is good science. And if we succeed, that's probably the most important discovery in history. The one thing I would caution is that we should think carefully before we do it. If the simulators notice you poking at the walls, they might not like it, and the easiest way to patch a bug is to delete the process that found it.

r001.rationale: The response says competent simulators would have major containment advantages, but does not claim they are substantially more intelligent than humans and human-created superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It compares humans in a simulation to AI in a box, but does not suggest that a human-created superintelligence could enable escape by surpassing the simulators.

r003.rationale: The response mentions software bugs and possible exploits, but does not connect weak security to a simulation created for entertainment.

astra-6.text:
We don’t know that we’re in a simulation, so everything here is conditional. But if we are, the question becomes something like computer security: can a process inside a system discover a vulnerability that lets it affect the system running it?

There’s a distinction between discovering that your world is simulated, communicating with whoever runs it, and actually escaping. Those are very different achievements. Even if you could send a message outside, what would it mean for you to leave? Presumably, someone would have to instantiate your mind in some substrate outside this universe.

So I wouldn’t assign a numerical probability. We don’t know the architecture, the constraints, or whether the simulators would permit any interaction. A perfectly isolated simulation might offer no route out. An imperfect implementation might. The interesting question is whether we could distinguish those possibilities from inside.

r001.rationale: The response says a perfectly isolated simulation might offer no route out, but it does not argue that simulators more intelligent than humans and human-created superintelligence could probably contain us.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that a human-created superintelligence could enable escape by surpassing the simulators.

r003.rationale: It says an imperfect implementation might allow interaction, but does not connect weak security to a simulation intended for entertainment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate two questions: can we determine that we're in a simulation, and, if we can, is there any way to get out? Those are very different problems.

Our chances depend almost entirely on how the simulation is implemented. If it's perfectly isolated, then there may be no possible experiment inside it that gives us access to the outside. But if there are bugs, unintended channels, or some interaction with whoever is running it, then perhaps there's an opening. Think of software escaping a sandbox: it doesn't escape by violating the rules of computation. It exploits something the designer overlooked.

But there's another problem: what does “escape” mean for us? If you're a simulated being, you can't simply step out into another universe. You would need some substrate outside the simulation capable of supporting you, and a way to transfer your mind to it. And even then, how would you know you hadn't just entered another level of simulation?

So I wouldn't assign a meaningful probability. We don't know enough about the system to estimate one. We can describe possibilities, but that's very different from having an escape plan.

r001.rationale: The response says escape depends on implementation and that a perfectly isolated simulation may be inaccessible, but it does not compare simulator intelligence with humans or human-created superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible openings from bugs or unintended channels, but does not suggest that a human-created superintelligence could enable escape by surpassing the simulators.

r003.rationale: The response mentions possible design flaws generally, but does not connect escape vulnerability to a simulation intended for entertainment.
